purpose: Why does the same display marker look smaller farther away?
meaning: In an ideal pinhole camera, a point at sideways coordinate X and positive depth z maps to virtual-image coordinate x=fX/z. A centered marker of real width W therefore has image width w=fW/z. Magnification m=f/z is dimensionless. Real dimensions remain fixed when depth changes; the changing projection is a measured image length rather than a shrinking object.

definition.setting: A photographer moves a straight display marker away from a pinhole. Its real width W stays measured in metres; its projection onto a fixed virtual image plane shrinks as depth z increases.

signature.z: Positive marker depth from the pinhole, in metres
signature.W: Real width of the centered marker, in metres
signature.f: Distance to the virtual image plane, in metres
signature.w: Projected marker width on that plane, in metres

conditions: The marker is centered, straight and parallel to the image plane. Use depth 2–10 m, real width 1–4 m and virtual image-plane distance 0.5–1.5 m, so the marker always lies beyond the plane. This point-pinhole model has no lens, finite aperture, sensor bounds or pixel calibration.
definition.domain_notes: Depth is 2–10 metres, marker width 1–4 metres and virtual image-plane distance 0.5–1.5 metres. Depth always exceeds the image-plane distance. This ideal point-pinhole construction uses a virtual plane in front of the pinhole; a physical rear image is inverted with the same width. The marker is parallel to the image plane and centered on the optical axis. Lens blur, pixels, distortion and field-of-view clipping are outside the model. Both scene directions share the same metre scale.

grammar.formation_rule: In an ideal pinhole camera, a point at sideways coordinate X and positive depth z maps to virtual-image coordinate x=fX/z. A centered marker of real width W therefore has image width w=fW/z. Magnification m=f/z is dimensionless. grammar.precedence: The ray from the pinhole to either endpoint intersects the virtual plane at the fraction f/z of its full depth. Its sideways displacement scales by the same factor. Subtract the two projected endpoint coordinates, f(W/2)/z and −f(W/2)/z, to obtain fW/z. Doubling depth halves this image width while leaving the real marker unchanged.
